Stiffhearted
STIF-har-ted
adj. (hard of heart; unyielding in will)
Hebrew chazaq leb, strong or hard of heart — the same verb used of Pharaoh's hardening. The Authorized Version's compound pairs it with impudent, literally hard of face, so that the prophet is sent to people hard in both the face they show and the heart behind it.

Biblical Definition

For they are impudent children and stiffhearted. I do send thee unto them; and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD. The commissioning of Ezekiel is unlike any other in Scripture for its candour about the outcome. God tells the prophet in advance that his hearers are hard, and the two words are a matched pair — impudent is literally hard of face, stiffhearted is hard of heart. Hard outside and hard within. Then comes the sentence that has steadied preachers ever since: I do send thee unto them, followed by the words he is to say, Thus saith the Lord GOD. The commission is not withdrawn because the ground is bad. God is explicit that the message will be refused — the house of Israel will not hearken unto thee; for they will not hearken unto me — and equally explicit that it must still be delivered: whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear. The prophet's success is defined by faithfulness in speaking, not by response in hearing. And God supplies what the task requires rather than removing the task: behold, I have made thy face strong against their faces, and thy forehead strong against their foreheads. The hardness is answered with a God-given firmness of the same kind, which is the only realistic provision for a man sent to people like this.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), under STIFF and HEARTED: obstinate; stubborn; not yielding to argument or persuasion; hard-hearted.

expand to see more

STIFFHEARTED, a. Obstinate; stubborn; contumacious.

STIFF, a. Not easily bent; rigid; not flexible; stubborn; not easily subdued or persuaded.

IMPUDENT, a. Shameless; wanting modesty; bold with contempt of others; saucy.

OBSTINATE, a. Stubborn; fixed firmly in resolution or purpose; not yielding to reason, arguments or other means.

HARDNESS, n. Obduracy; impenitence; confirmed state of wickedness.

Key Scripture

Ezekiel 2:4 — "For they are impudent children and stiffhearted. I do send thee unto them; and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD."

Ezekiel 2:5 — "And they, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear, (for they are a rebellious house,) yet shall know that there hath been a prophet among them."

Ezekiel 3:7 — "But the house of Israel will not hearken unto thee; for they will not hearken unto me: for all the house of Israel are impudent and hardhearted."

Ezekiel 3:8 — "Behold, I have made thy face strong against their faces, and thy forehead strong against their foreheads."

Modern Corruption

Ministry is now widely evaluated by response, so that resistance is read as a failure of method; Ezekiel is told the response in advance and sent anyway, with faithfulness defined as speaking.

expand to see more

Where the effectiveness of preaching is measured by visible result, a congregation that does not respond becomes evidence that the preacher must change something — his tone, his approach, his emphasis. The pragmatic instinct then does what it always does and adjusts the message until the response improves. Ezekiel 2 forecloses the reasoning at the outset. God names the hardness, predicts the refusal, and commissions the prophet in the same breath, giving as the measure of the mission not conversion but this: yet shall know that there hath been a prophet among them. A faithful man may labour among stiffhearted people for a lifetime and have discharged his commission exactly.

The passage cuts the other way as well, against a hardness the preacher himself may acquire. God does not tell Ezekiel to become contemptuous of his hearers; he makes the prophet's forehead strong, which is endurance rather than scorn, and the same prophet is later shown weeping and sitting astonished among the captives seven days. A minister who has learned to expect resistance is in danger of welcoming it as proof of his soundness, and of mistaking a hard manner for a strong forehead. The Lord looked on a city that would not receive him and wept over it, having already pronounced its judgment. Both belong together.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chazaq (H2389), strong, hard; leb (H3820), heart; qasheh (H7186), stiff, stubborn; metsach (H4696), forehead.

expand to see more

Hebrew chazaq leb (H2389, H3820) — hard of heart; rendered stiffhearted.

Hebrew qasheh (H7186) — hard, stiff, severe; the root behind stiffnecked throughout the Pentateuch.

Hebrew metsach (H4696) — forehead, brow; hard in them, made strong in the prophet.

Hebrew panim (H6440) — face; impudent is literally hard of face.

Hebrew mariy (H4805) — rebellion; a rebellious house, the standing description in Ezekiel.

Usage

"“impudent children and stiffhearted” — hard in face and heart alike."

"“I do send thee unto them” — the commission given with the warning."

"“I have made thy face strong against their faces” — the provision, not the exemption."
